questions.text: Mention the relations of the pituitary gland and its clinical importance.
questions.explanation: The pituitary's location in the sella turcica makes it vulnerable to mass effects.
questions.keyConcept: Spatial relations determine clinical manifestations of pituitary tumors.
questions.modelAnswer:
Relations:
- Anterior: Body of sphenoid and tuberculum sellae
- Posterior: Dorsum sellae, basilar artery, pons
- Laterally: Cavernous sinus and its contents (CN III, IV, V1, V2, internal carotid artery)
- Superiorly: Diaphragm sellae (separates from optic chiasma)
- Inferiorly: Body of sphenoid with air sinuses (separates from nasopharynx)
Clinical importance (pituitary tumor):
- Upward compression of optic chiasma → bitemporal hemianopia
- Downward compression → ballooning of sella turcica
- Lateral pressure on cavernous sinus → eye congestion, diplopia
- Endocrinal disturbances (hypopituitarism or hormone excess)

questions.text: Mention the relations of the pituitary gland and its clinical importance.
questions.explanation: The pituitary's location in the sella turcica makes mass effects predictable.
questions.keyConcept: Spatial relations determine clinical manifestations of pituitary tumors.
questions.modelAnswer:
Relations:
- Anterior: Tuberculum sellae
- Posterior: Dorsum sellae, basilar artery, pons
- Superior: Diaphragma sellae (separates from optic chiasma)
- Inferior: Body of sphenoid & sphenoidal air sinus
- Lateral: Cavernous sinus with its contents (CN III, IV, V1, V2, internal carotid artery)
Clinical importance (pituitary tumor):
- Upward compression → bitemporal hemianopia
- Downward compression → ballooning of sella turcica
- Lateral pressure → eye congestion, diplopia
- Endocrinal disturbances

questions.text: Enumerate the blood supply of the pituitary gland.
questions.explanation: The portal system connects hypothalamus to anterior pituitary.
questions.keyConcept: Superior hypophyseal arteries supply the portal system.
questions.modelAnswer:
Arterial supply:
- Superior hypophyseal arteries (from internal carotid)
- Inferior hypophyseal artery (from internal carotid)
Venous drainage:
- Cavernous sinus

questions.text: What is the origin and development of the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: Adenohypophysis from oral ectoderm, neurohypophysis from neural ectoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Dual origin: Rathke's pouch + infundibulum.
questions.modelAnswer:
Origin: Ectodermal (two primordia).
Development:
- Hypophysial (Rathke's pouch): upward diverticulum from stomodeal ectoderm → forms adenohypophysis.
- Neurohypophysial (infundibular process): downward diverticulum from diencephalon → forms neurohypophysis.

questions.text: Enumerate the anomalies of the pituitary gland.
questions.explanation: Remnants of Rathke's pouch can give rise to tumors or ectopic tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Craniopharyngioma is the most common suprasellar tumor in children.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Pharyngeal hypophysis (ectopic anterior pituitary tissue)
- Craniopharyngioma (Rathke's pouch remnant)

questions.text: Compare between the adenohypophysis and neurohypophysis of the pituitary gland.
questions.explanation: The two lobes differ in origin, structure, and function.
questions.keyConcept: Adenohypophysis synthesizes hormones; neurohypophysis stores hypothalamic hormones.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Adenohypophysis | Neurohypophysis |
|---------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin | Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm) | Infundibulum (neuroectoderm) |
| Parts | Pars distalis, pars intermedia, pars tuberalis | Pars nervosa, infundibular stalk |
| Cell types | Chromophobes, acidophils, basophils | Pituicytes (glial) |
| Hormones | GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH | ADH, oxytocin (stored, not synthesized) |
| Connection to hypothalamus | Vascular (portal) | Neural (hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract) |

questions.text: Describe the effects of pituitary tumors.
questions.explanation: Tumor effects depend on direction of expansion and hormone secretion.
questions.keyConcept: Mass effect and hormone excess/deficit define clinical presentation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Upward pressure: optic chiasma compression → bitemporal hemianopia.
Downward pressure: ballooning of sella turcica.
Lateral pressure: cavernous sinus involvement → eye congestion, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia.
Endocrine disturbances: hypersecretion (e.g., prolactin, GH, ACTH) or hypopituitarism.

questions.text: Which of the following is a part of adenohypophysis?
questions.explanation: The adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) consists of pars distalis, pars tuberalis, and pars intermedia. Pars intermedia is present in some species; in humans it is rudimentary but still considered part of adenohypophysis.

questions.text: Anatomically, the posterior lobe of pituitary gland DOESN'T include:
questions.explanation: The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) includes the median eminence, infundibular stalk, and pars nervosa. Pars distalis is part of the anterior pituitary.

questions.text: Choose the true statement about hypophyseal arteries:
questions.explanation: Superior hypophyseal arteries arise from the internal carotid artery (fourth part) and contribute to the hypophyseal portal system.
options: There is single superior hypophyseal artery.
There are multiple inferior hypophyseal arteries.
Superior hypophyseal arteries branch from 4th part of ICA.
Superior hypophyseal arteries form infundibular arterial ring.

questions.text: Venous drainage of the pituitary gland ends into ............. sinus.
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland drains into the cavernous sinus, which is a major venous channel on each side of the sella turcica.

questions.text: Infundibular process develops from:
questions.explanation: The infundibular process (future posterior pituitary) develops as a downgrowth from the floor of the diencephalon (neural ectoderm).

questions.text: The infundibular recess of the 3rd ventricle is derived from:
questions.explanation: The infundibular recess is an extension of the third ventricle into the upper part of the infundibulum (neural stalk).

questions.text: The sella turcica, which lodges the pituitary gland, is located in the:
questions.explanation: The sella turcica is a saddle-shaped depression in the body of the sphenoid bone that houses the pituitary gland.

questions.text: Which anatomical structure is located as a direct lateral relation to the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus lies on each side of the sella turcica and is directly lateral to the pituitary gland.

questions.text: The pituitary gland is directly related anteriorly to which of the following bony structures?
questions.explanation: Anteriorly, the pituitary gland is related to the tuberculum sellae, a bony elevation anterior to the sella turcica.

questions.text: The inferior relation of the pituitary gland consists of which of the following anatomical structures?
questions.explanation: Inferiorly, the pituitary gland lies on the body of the sphenoid bone, which contains the sphenoidal air sinus.
options: Body of sphenoid and sphenoidal air sinus

questions.text: Compression of the cavernous sinus by a laterally expanding pituitary tumour is most likely to present with which clinical signs?
questions.explanation: Cavernous sinus compression affects cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, causing diplopia (due to extraocular muscle palsies) and venous congestion (proptosis, chemosis).

questions.text: Diplopia and venous congestion in the eye may result from:
questions.explanation: Pituitary tumors extending laterally compress the cavernous sinus, causing ophthalmoplegia (diplopia) and impaired venous drainage (congestion).
options: Compression of the optic nerve by the frontal lobe
Pressure of the pituitary gland on the cavernous sinus
Obstruction of the central retinal artery
Lesion of the oculomotor nerve in the orbit

questions.text: Pituitary adenoma may affect the visual field resulting in?
questions.explanation: Suprasellar extension compresses the optic chiasm, affecting crossing nasal retinal fibers, leading to bitemporal hemianopia.

questions.text: During embryological development, the infundibular process (which gives rise to the posterior pituitary) arises as a downward outgrowth from which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) develops from the floor of the diencephalon, specifically the infundibulum.
options: Roof of the oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch)
Neural crest of the pharyngeal arches

questions.text: Which structure in the adult human body develops directly from the embryonic Rathke's pouch?
questions.explanation: Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal outpouching of the stomodeum that gives rise to the anterior pituitary (pars distalis, pars intermedia, pars tuberalis).

questions.text: Which adult structure is derived from Rathke's pouch?
questions.explanation: Rathke's pouch gives rise to the adenohypophysis, primarily the pars distalis, pars intermedia, and pars tuberalis.

questions.text: Pituitary cleft lies between?
questions.explanation: The pituitary (Rathke's) cleft is a remnant of the original Rathke's pouch lumen, located between the pars distalis and pars intermedia.

questions.text: Compare between acidophils and basophils.
questions.explanation: Acidophils and basophils are anterior pituitary cell types distinguished by staining and hormones.
questions.keyConcept: Staining affinity correlates with hormone content.
questions.modelAnswer:
Characteristic          | Acidophils               | Basophils
% of pituitary cells    | 35%                      | 15%
Size                    | Smaller                  | Larger
LM stain                | Acidic (e.g., eosin)     | Basic (e.g., H&E)
PAS reaction            | Negative                 | Positive
Granules (LM)           | Large                    | Small, less numerous
TEM features            | RER, Golgi, mitochondria, large granules | RER, Golgi, mitochondria, small granules (variable density)
Hormones produced       | GH, prolactin            | TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH

questions.text: Compare between acidophils and basophils in the anterior pituitary.
questions.explanation: Staining affinity correlates with hormone content.
questions.keyConcept: Acidophils → GH/prolactin; basophils → TSH/ACTH/FSH/LH.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Acidophils | Basophils |
|---------|------------|-----------|
| % of cells | ~35% | ~15% |
| LM stain | Acidic (eosin, orange G) | Basic (H&E, PAS positive) |
| Granules (LM) | Large | Small, less numerous |
| Hormones | GH, prolactin | TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH |

questions.text: Describe the LM and EM structure of somatotrophs.
questions.explanation: Somatotrophs are the most numerous acidophils.
questions.keyConcept: GH-secreting cells have large, dense granules.
questions.modelAnswer:
LM: Acidophilic, large closely packed granules.
EM: Dense secretory granules (300-400 nm), well-developed rER and Golgi.
Function: Secrete growth hormone (GH) which stimulates IGF-1 production → bone and soft tissue growth.

questions.text: Describe the structure and function of pars intermedia.
questions.explanation: Pars intermedia is better developed in lower animals.
questions.keyConcept: MSH production is minimal in adult humans.
questions.modelAnswer:
Structure: Thin sheet of basophilic cells (corticotroph-like) separated from pars distalis by the pituitary cleft; often contains colloid-filled Rathke cysts.
Function: Secretes POMC-derived peptides (ACTH, lipotropin, MSH). In humans, largely rudimentary.

questions.text: What are Herring bodies and where are they found?
questions.explanation: Visible on light microscopy as eosinophilic structures.
questions.keyConcept: Herring bodies = hormone storage in posterior pituitary.
questions.modelAnswer: Herring bodies are dilated terminal axons in the pars nervosa (posterior pituitary) that contain aggregates of neurosecretory granules (ADH or oxytocin) and neurophysins. They represent storage sites for posterior pituitary hormones.

questions.text: Which of the following characterizes the endocrine glands?
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands are highly vascularized with fenestrated capillaries to allow easy passage of hormones into the bloodstream.
options: Are formed of groups of storage cells.

questions.text: Steroid hormone secreting cells are characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Steroid hormone synthesis requires abundant smooth ER (for cholesterol side-chain cleavage and further modifications) and mitochondria with tubular cristae.
options: Hormones come outside the cell through secretory vesicles.

questions.text: A characteristic feature of steroid-secreting cells is:
questions.explanation: Steroidogenic cells contain abundant smooth ER and lipid droplets (cholesterol esters) in their cytoplasm.
options: High lipid content and smooth ER

questions.text: All of the following characterizes the peptide secreting cells EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Peptide-secreting cells have abundant RER and Golgi, not abundant SER. SER is characteristic of steroid-secreting cells.
options: Presence of specific receptors on cell membrane

questions.text: Peptide hormones differ from steroid hormones in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Peptide hormones are synthesized on RER and processed in the Golgi, which is prominent. Steroid hormones are synthesized in SER/mitochondria.

questions.text: All of the following hormones are classified as amino acid hormones EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone derived from cholesterol. Thyroid hormones and catecholamines are derived from amino acids (tyrosine).

questions.text: The steroid hormones are formed by metabolism of cholesterol in which of the following organelles?
questions.explanation: Steroidogenesis begins in mitochondria (cholesterol → pregnenolone) and continues in smooth ER.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a pure endocrine gland?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland is a pure endocrine gland (no exocrine function). Pancreas, thyroid, ovary have mixed or exocrine functions.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a mixed endocrine gland?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland has both endocrine (follicular cells, C cells) and exocrine-like activity (follicle lumen storage), but is typically classified as endocrine; however, among the options, thyroid is often called mixed because it stores colloid extracellularly. Parathyroid is purely endocrine.

questions.text: Ghrelin hormone is produced mainly by which of the following organs?
questions.explanation: Ghrelin is primarily produced by P/D1 cells in the gastric fundus.

questions.text: Atrial natriuretic factor is produced by which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: ANP is synthesized and secreted by atrial myocytes in response to atrial stretch.

questions.text: Which of the following cells is responsible for differentiation of T-thymocytes?
questions.explanation: Thymic epithelial reticular cells produce thymic hormones (thymosin, thymopoietin) that promote T-cell maturation.

questions.text: Which of the following cells secrete a substance that acts as a releasing hormone for growth hormone secretion?
questions.explanation: Enteroendocrine cells of the gut secrete ghrelin, which stimulates GH release from the pituitary.

questions.text: Which of the following substances stimulates appetite?
questions.explanation: Ghrelin is an orexigenic hormone that increases appetite and food intake.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is considered a satiety factor?
questions.explanation: Leptin, produced by adipocytes, signals satiety to the hypothalamus.

questions.text: All of the following are characteristic of the granules of Atrial Natriuretic Factor EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Atrial myocytes have well-developed Golgi complexes for ANP synthesis; they are not 'small'.
options: Present at the periphery of the cell

questions.text: Which of the following substances participates in regulating new adipose tissue formation?
questions.explanation: Leptin regulates energy balance and influences adipogenesis.

questions.text: Which of the following cells stimulates the formation of red blood cells?
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney secrete erythropoietin (EPO) in response to hypoxia, stimulating RBC production.

questions.text: Which of the following cells control blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin (increases BP); atrial myocytes secrete ANP (decreases BP).

questions.text: Mode of secretion of substances that act only on nearby target cells is considered:
questions.explanation: Paracrine signaling acts on adjacent cells via diffusion through interstitial fluid.

questions.text: A pregnant lady has hormonal level changes in her body to regulate the different stages of her pregnancy. What type of signals are being used to release these hormones into her body?
questions.explanation: Hormones released into the bloodstream to act on distant targets constitute endocrine signaling.

questions.text: Mode of secretion of substances released when signaling molecules on the surface of one cell affect a target cell in direct contact is called:
questions.explanation: Juxtacrine signaling requires direct membrane-membrane contact (e.g., Delta-Notch).

questions.text: Mode of secretion of substances from cells that act on themselves is considered:
questions.explanation: Autocrine signaling occurs when a cell secretes a factor that binds to receptors on its own surface.

questions.text: A process in which a hormone acts on the cell of origin without entering blood circulation is called:
questions.explanation: Autocrine action: the hormone acts on the same cell that produced it.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: Stress activates the HPA axis, altering pituitary secretion (e.g., ACTH).
options: Is considered as subsidiary organizer of endocrine system.
Its secretion is altered by stress.
Exercise and day time have no effect on its secretion.
It is enclosed by the blood brain barrier.

questions.text: Pituitary gland is considered the master of endocrine glands because:
questions.explanation: The anterior pituitary secretes tropic hormones that regulate thyroid, adrenals, and gonads.
options: It is connected directly to the hypothalamus.
It is formed of adeno- and neurohypophysis.
It is located outside the blood brain barrier.
It receives negative feedback regulation from their target organ hormones.
It controls the activity of other endocrine glands.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The pituitary lies in the sella turcica, a bony cavity, not membranous.
options: Lies in a membranous cavity called Sella Turcica.
Its pars distalis is connected to hypothalamus by tuberoinfundibular stalk.
Its roof covering is formed by dura mater and fibrous capsule.

questions.text: Adenohypophysis differs from neurohypophysis by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Adenohypophysis includes pars distalis, pars tuberalis, and pars intermedia; neurohypophysis includes pars nervosa and infundibulum.
options: Embryologically it represents down growth from the floor of the hypothalamus.
Is connected to the hypothalamus by infundibular stalk.
Pars tuberalis is part of its component.
Formed of pars nervosa and infundibular stalk.
It is the neural component of the pituitary gland.

questions.text: Which is TRUE about adenohypophysis?
questions.explanation: Adenohypophysis develops from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm).
options: Embryologically, it develops from Rathke's pouch.
Is connected to the hypothalamus by infundibular stalk.
Formed of pars nervosa and infundibular stalk.
It is the neural component of the pituitary gland.

questions.text: Cells of pars distalis belong to which of the following categories?
questions.explanation: Pars distalis cells are epithelial cells arranged in cords and follicles.

questions.text: Which of the following types of capillaries are present in the pars distalis of pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The anterior pituitary has fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms to facilitate hormone exchange.

questions.text: Pars distalis constitutes what percentage of the total volume of pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: Pars distalis makes up approximately 75% of the pituitary gland's volume.

questions.text: Chromophobes differ from chromophils in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Chromophobes have few or no secretory granules and appear pale under H&E.

questions.text: Which of the following cells are phagocytic?
questions.explanation: Follicular stellate cells are non-endocrine, phagocytic cells in the anterior pituitary.

questions.text: Which of the following cells is characterized by multiple cytoplasmic processes connected by gap junctions?
questions.explanation: Follicular stellate cells form a network via gap junctions, regulating paracrine signaling.

questions.text: The processes of follicular stellate cells in the pars distalis are connected mainly by:
questions.explanation: Gap junctions allow intercellular communication among follicular stellate cells.

questions.text: Acidophils differ from basophils in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Acidophils (somatotrophs, lactotrophs) are PAS-negative because their granules are not glycoprotein-rich, unlike basophils.
options: Are situated peripherally in pars distalis
The size of their cells is 15-25 um

questions.text: Regarding acidophils of pituitary, which is true?
questions.explanation: Acidophil granules are not stained by PAS (periodic acid-Schiff).
options: They are less numerous than basophils.

questions.text: Basophils are characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Basophils (thyrotrophs, gonadotrophs, corticotrophs) contain glycoprotein hormones that are PAS-positive.
options: 35% of total cells of pars distalis

questions.text: Which of the following cells are PAS positive?
questions.explanation: Thyrotrophs (TSH) and gonadotrophs (FSH, LH) secrete glycoproteins and are PAS-positive.

questions.text: Which of the following cells of pars distalis have the smallest granules?
questions.explanation: Thyrotrophs contain the smallest secretory granules (100-150 nm).

questions.text: When examining the parenchymal cells of the anterior pituitary gland via electron microscopy, which of the following cell types is characteristically identified by possessing the smallest secretory granules?** ★
questions.explanation: Thyrotropes have the smallest secretory granules (100-150 nm).

questions.text: The smallest granules are present in which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Thyrotrophs have the smallest granules.

questions.text: Which of the following cells of pars distalis have granules that increase in size during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Mammotrophs (lactotrophs) hypertrophy and increase granule size during pregnancy due to elevated estrogen.

questions.text: Which of the following cells of pars distalis show large and closely packed granules?
questions.explanation: Mammotrophs contain large (600-700 nm), dense granules.

questions.text: Which of the following cells of pars distalis secrete prolactin?
questions.explanation: Mammotrophs (lactotrophs) secrete prolactin.

questions.text: Which of the following cells of pars distalis secrete growth hormone?
questions.explanation: Somatotrophs secrete growth hormone (GH).

questions.text: Somatotrophs are characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Somatotroph granules stain orange with orange G (acidophilic).
options: Their granules are stained with orange G stain.
Their cytoplasm contains few rER and Golgi apparatus.

questions.text: Somatotrophs differ from mammotrophs in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Somatotrophs stain orange with orange G; mammotrophs stain red with erythrosin.
options: Their granules are about 200 nm in diameter.
They constitute 20% of total secretory cells of pars distalis.
Their granules are stained red by erythrocin.
Their granules are stained orange by orange G.

questions.text: Follicle stimulating hormone is secreted by which of the following cells of pars distalis?
questions.explanation: Gonadotrophs secrete FSH and LH.

questions.text: Adrenocorticotrophic hormone is secreted by which of the following cells of pars distalis?
questions.explanation: Corticotrophs secrete ACTH and MSH.

questions.text: Which of the following cells secrete hormones that help in induction of ovulation and differentiation of corpus luteum?
questions.explanation: Gonadotrophs secrete FSH (follicle development) and LH (ovulation, corpus luteum).

questions.text: Thyrotrophs differ from gonadotrophs in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Thyrotrophs have the smallest granules (100-150 nm), while gonadotrophs have larger granules.
options: Constitute 10% of total pars distalis secretory cells.
Granules are of variable electron densities.

questions.text: Gonadotrophs differ from corticotrophs in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Gonadotrophs are PAS-positive due to glycoprotein hormones; corticotrophs (ACTH) are PAS-negative.
options: Constitute 20% of total pars distalis secretory cells.
Granules are of variable size and electron density.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is Not True about neurosecretory cells?
questions.explanation: Neurosecretory cells regulate the anterior pituitary via releasing hormones, not the pars nervosa directly.
options: Scattered in different sites in the hypothalamus.
Their axons form the tuberoinfundibular tract.
Their hormones share in induction of labor.
Their secretions regulate cells of pars nervosa.

questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the histological features of thyrotropes in the pars distalis?
questions.explanation: Thyrotropes contain small PAS-positive granules (glycoprotein TSH).
options: They possess small granules that are PAS positive.
They represent the most abundant cell type.

questions.text: Pituicytes are best described as:
questions.explanation: Pituicytes are glial-like support cells in the posterior pituitary, positive for GFAP.
options: Modified epithelial cells that secrete hormones
Endocrine cells of the anterior pituitary

questions.text: Pituicytes, the supportive cells of the neurohypophysis, uniquely stain positive for which of the following markers?
questions.explanation: Pituicytes express GFAP, a marker for glial cells.

questions.text: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers is typically positive in Pituicytes?
questions.explanation: GFAP is a specific marker for pituicytes (modified glia).

questions.text: Which of the following statements characterizes pituicytes of pars nervosa?
questions.explanation: Pituicytes are GFAP-positive glial cells.
options: It can be stained by Sudan III.

questions.text: The neurosecretions secreted by magnocellular neurons are carried along the axons of hypothalamo-hypophyseal tracts to be stored in:
questions.explanation: Herring bodies are axonal dilations in the posterior pituitary where ADH and oxytocin are stored.

questions.text: What are Herring bodies, as seen in the pars nervosa?
questions.explanation: Herring bodies are swellings filled with neurosecretory granules containing ADH or oxytocin.
options: Calcified concretions in the pineal gland
Large aggregations of secretory granules containing vasopressin and oxytocin
Capillary networks of the portal system

questions.text: Herring bodies contain which of the following hormones?
questions.explanation: Herring bodies store oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH).

questions.text: Pars nervosa Does Not contain:
questions.explanation: The pars nervosa contains axons and pituicytes, but no nerve cell bodies (those are in hypothalamus).

questions.text: Which of the following truly describes Rathke's cysts of pars tuberalis?
questions.explanation: Rathke's cysts are remnants of Rathke's pouch, lined by cuboidal epithelium and contain colloid.
options: Colloid-containing cysts lined by cuboidal cells.
Mucus-containing cysts lined by squamous cells.
Serous-containing cysts lined by columnar cells.
Muco-serous containing cysts lined by columnar cells.
Vacuolated cysts lined by squamous cells.

questions.text: Neurosecretions stored in Herring bodies in pars nervosa regulate which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin acts on mammary gland (milk ejection); ADH acts on renal collecting tubules (water reabsorption).

questions.text: Light microscopic examination shows a faintly acidophilic structure which shows large aggregation of secretory granules by E/M. Which of the following best suits this description?
questions.explanation: Herring bodies appear as eosinophilic (acidophilic) structures on LM and contain aggregated secretory granules on EM.

questions.text: Primary capillary plexus of hypophyseal portal system differs from secondary capillary plexus in which of the following?
questions.explanation: The primary plexus in the median eminence is drained by portal veins that carry blood to the secondary plexus in the pars distalis.
options: Hormones leave them to be distributed to the parenchymal cells.
They are drained by hypophyseal portal veins.
They are coming from inferior hypophyseal artery.

questions.text: The adenohypophysis is directly supplied by which of the following circulatory systems?
questions.explanation: The anterior pituitary receives its blood supply via the hypophyseal portal system, not directly from systemic arteries.

questions.text: Releasing hormones from the hypothalamus reach the anterior pituitary through which of the following?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic releasing hormones travel via the hypophyseal portal veins to the anterior pituitary.

questions.text: What's true concerning the connection between hypothalamus and pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The adenohypophysis is connected via the hypophyseal portal system, not by direct neural connection.
options: Infundibulum connects hypothalamus with anterior lobe
Adenohypophysis connected by Hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal veins

questions.text: Which cell type is the most abundant within the pars distalis of the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: Somatotropes (GH-secreting cells) constitute about 40-50% of anterior pituitary cells, making them the most abundant.

questions.text: Discuss hormone receptor locations and significance.
questions.explanation: Membrane receptors trigger rapid second messenger cascades; intracellular receptors directly influence gene transcription (slower but more prolonged).
questions.keyConcept: Receptor location dictates signaling mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer:
Receptors are either:
- Membrane-bound (for hydrophilic hormones), or
- Intracellular (for lipophilic hormones).
Their location determines the mechanism of action and speed of response.

questions.text: Distinguish between hydrophilic and lipophilic hormones.
questions.explanation: Solubility affects transport, receptor location, and onset of action.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical nature determines transport and mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer:
Hydrophilic hormones (peptides, catecholamines):
- Water-soluble, circulate freely, act on membrane receptors.
Lipophilic hormones (steroids, thyroid hormones):
- Fat-soluble, require carrier proteins, act on intracellular receptors.

questions.text: Describe the hypothalamo-pituitary axis.
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic hormones control the pituitary, which controls peripheral endocrine glands.
questions.keyConcept: Functional unit connecting CNS to endocrine system.
questions.modelAnswer:
The hypothalamo-pituitary axis links the nervous and endocrine systems.
- Hypothalamus secretes releasing/inhibiting hormones that regulate anterior pituitary via portal circulation.
- Posterior pituitary hormones are synthesized in hypothalamic nuclei and transported through neural pathways.

questions.text: List hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones.
questions.explanation: Each releasing hormone stimulates a specific anterior pituitary hormone; inhibiting hormones suppress them.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamic peptides regulate pituitary secretion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Releasing: TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH.
Inhibiting: Somatostatin (inhibits GH), Dopamine (inhibits prolactin).

questions.text: Define signal transduction and describe the three major stages of the process.
questions.explanation: A fundamental concept in endocrinology and cellular communication.
questions.keyConcept: Conversion of extracellular signal into cellular response.
questions.modelAnswer:
Signal transduction is the process by which external stimuli, detected by a receptor, are converted into an intracellular action.
Three stages:
1. Reception – signal binds to receptor.
2. Transduction – signal carried through a pathway.
3. Response – activation of cellular changes (enzyme activity, gene expression, etc.).

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of the cAMP second messenger system.
questions.explanation: cAMP is a classic second messenger for many hormones (e.g., epinephrine, glucagon).
questions.keyConcept: G-protein activation leads to cAMP production and PKA activation.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Hormone binds to GPCR → GDP replaced with GTP on G-alpha subunit.
2. If Gs is involved, adenylyl cyclase (AC) is activated → converts ATP to cAMP.
3. cAMP activates Protein Kinase A (PKA) → phosphorylates cellular proteins.
4. In nucleus, active PKA phosphorylates CREB → binds to CRE → activates gene transcription.

questions.text: Explain the concepts of specificity and amplification in signaling systems.
questions.explanation: Specificity ensures correct target cells respond; amplification allows a few hormone molecules to produce a large response.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor distribution ensures specificity; cascades amplify signals.
questions.modelAnswer:
Specificity: Precise molecular complementarity between signal and receptor; receptors only present in certain cell types.
Amplification: Enzyme cascades where one activated enzyme activates many molecules of a second enzyme → geometric increase in signal.

questions.text: Name the clinical conditions resulting from disturbances in Growth Hormone (GH) secretion. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The effect of GH excess or deficiency depends on the age of onset.
questions.keyConcept: Timing of GH excess determines linear vs. acral growth.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Gigantism (excess GH before puberty)
- Acromegaly (excess GH after puberty)
- Dwarfism (GH deficiency in children)

questions.text: Mention 4 factors that stimulate secretion of Growth Hormone (GH). (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: GH secretion is stimulated by low blood glucose, high amino acids, and stress.
questions.keyConcept: GH release increases during catabolic states.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Deficiency of energy substrates (hypoglycemia, starvation, fasting, exercise)
2. Stressful stimuli
3. Increased blood amino acids after a protein meal
4. Glucagon

questions.text: Discuss the metabolic effects of growth hormone.
questions.explanation: GH shifts metabolism toward using fats for energy while sparing glucose, raising blood sugar.
questions.keyConcept: GH promotes lipolysis, protein synthesis, and insulin resistance.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Carbohydrates: Anti-insulin effect → blood glucose increases.
- Proteins: Anabolic → increased amino acid uptake & protein synthesis.
- Fats: Lipolytic → increased free fatty acids and ketone production.

questions.text: Explain the diabetogenic effect of GH.
questions.explanation: Chronic GH excess can lead to secondary diabetes due to impaired insulin action.
questions.keyConcept: GH antagonizes insulin action, raising blood glucose.
questions.modelAnswer: GH decreases glucose uptake in tissues and increases hepatic glucose production, causing insulin resistance and hyperglycemia.

questions.text: Describe the clinical conditions resulting from disturbances in prolactin secretion, including their primary causes and manifestations. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: Prolactin inhibits gonadotropin release, explaining reproductive dysfunction in hyperprolactinemia.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperprolactinemia causes hypogonadism and galactorrhea.
questions.modelAnswer:
[A] Hyperprolactinemia:
- Causes: anterior pituitary tumors or hypothalamic destruction.
- Manifestations: females – amenorrhea, galactorrhea, sterility; males – hypogonadism, sterility, impotence.
[B] Hypoprolactinemia (rare):
- Cause: rare.
- Manifestation: inability to lactate after labor.

questions.text: Mention Oxytocin effects on pregnant and non-pregnant women. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: Oxytocin has roles in reproduction beyond parturition and lactation.
questions.keyConcept: Oxytocin stimulates uterine and myoepithelial contraction.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pregnant women:
1. Labor – stimulates uterine contraction.
2. Milk ejection – contraction of myoepithelial cells (milk let-down reflex).
Non-pregnant women:
1. Semen transport – aids transport from vagina to uterus during intercourse.

questions.text: Describe the milk let-down reflex.
questions.explanation: A classic neuroendocrine reflex; oxytocin is the key hormone.
questions.keyConcept: Suckling triggers oxytocin release and milk ejection.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Nipple stimulation activates sensory nerves.
2. Impulses reach hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei.
3. Oxytocin released from posterior pituitary.
4. Oxytocin causes contraction of myoepithelial cells.
5. Milk ejected into ducts.

questions.text: Describe volume regulation of ADH secretion.
questions.explanation: ADH is primarily regulated by plasma osmolality, but severe hypovolemia overrides osmotic control.
questions.keyConcept: Hemodynamic changes strongly stimulate ADH release.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Significant hypovolemia (15–25% blood loss) reduces atrial stretch receptor activity → removes inhibitory signals → increases ADH release.
- Baroreceptors also contribute.
- ADH restores volume by water retention and vasoconstriction.

questions.text: Define signal transduction and describe its three major stages.
questions.explanation: Fundamental concept in endocrinology.
questions.keyConcept: Reception → transduction → response.
questions.modelAnswer:
Signal transduction = conversion of an extracellular signal into an intracellular response.
Stages:
1. Reception – ligand binds to receptor.
2. Transduction – signal relayed via second messengers or cascades.
3. Response – cellular effect (enzyme activation, gene transcription, etc.).

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of the cAMP second messenger system.
questions.explanation: cAMP is a classic second messenger for many hormones (e.g., glucagon, epinephrine).
questions.keyConcept: GPCR → Gs → AC → cAMP → PKA.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Hormone binds to Gs-coupled receptor → GDP replaced by GTP on Gsα.
2. Gsα activates adenylyl cyclase → ATP → cAMP.
3. cAMP activates PKA → phosphorylates target proteins.
4. PKA can translocate to nucleus and phosphorylate CREB → gene transcription.

questions.text: Compare between up‑regulation and down‑regulation of hormone receptors.
questions.explanation: Cells adjust receptor density to modulate responsiveness.
questions.keyConcept: Up = more sensitive; down = less sensitive.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Up‑regulation | Down‑regulation |
|---------|---------------|-----------------|
| Definition | Increase in receptor number | Decrease in receptor number |
| Effect on sensitivity | Increases sensitivity to hormone | Decreases sensitivity |
| Mechanism | Prolonged exposure to low hormone or antagonist | Prolonged exposure to high hormone (homologous desensitization) |

questions.text: List the hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary and their primary targets.
questions.explanation: Anterior pituitary is the master gland.
questions.keyConcept: Each tropic hormone controls a peripheral endocrine gland.
questions.modelAnswer:
- GH → liver, bone, soft tissues (via IGF-1)
- Prolactin → mammary glands
- TSH → thyroid
- ACTH → adrenal cortex
- FSH → gonads (follicle/spermatogenesis)
- LH → gonads (ovulation/testosterone)

questions.text: Mention the factors that stimulate growth hormone (GH) secretion.
questions.explanation: GH release is increased during catabolic states.
questions.keyConcept: Low glucose and high amino acids stimulate GH.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Hypoglycemia, fasting, starvation
- Exercise
- Stress (surgery, trauma, fever)
- Increased blood amino acids (arginine)
- Glucagon
- GHRH (hypothalamus)
- Ghrelin

questions.text: Discuss the metabolic effects of growth hormone.
questions.explanation: GH shifts metabolism toward fat utilization, sparing glucose.
questions.keyConcept: GH promotes lipolysis, protein synthesis, and insulin resistance.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Carbohydrate metabolism: anti-insulin → increases blood glucose (diabetogenic).
- Protein metabolism: anabolic → increases amino acid uptake and protein synthesis.
- Fat metabolism: lipolytic → increases free fatty acids and ketogenesis.

questions.text: Describe the clinical features of acromegaly.
questions.explanation: Excess GH after epiphyseal closure causes acral and soft tissue overgrowth.
questions.keyConcept: Acromegaly = post‑pubertal GH excess.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Enlarged hands and feet
- Coarse facial features (prognathism, broad nose)
- Thickened skin, hyperhidrosis
- Organomegaly (heart, liver, kidneys)
- Kyphosis, arthropathy
- Hypertension, glucose intolerance
- Visual field defects (if macroadenoma)

questions.text: Explain the milk‑let‑down reflex.
questions.explanation: A classic neuroendocrine reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Suckling → oxytocin release → milk ejection.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Nipple stimulation (suckling) → sensory impulses to spinal cord → hypothalamus.
2. Paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei release oxytocin from posterior pituitary.
3. Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells of breast alveoli and ducts → milk ejection.

questions.text: What are the renal and extra‑renal effects of ADH?
questions.explanation: ADH is primarily antidiuretic but also vasopressor at high doses.
questions.keyConcept: V2 = water reabsorption; V1 = vasoconstriction/ACTH.
questions.modelAnswer:
Renal (V2 receptors): increases aquaporin‑2 insertion in collecting duct → water reabsorption → concentrated urine.
Extra‑renal:
- V1a receptors (vascular smooth muscle): vasoconstriction → increased BP.
- V1b (V3) receptors (anterior pituitary): increase ACTH secretion.

questions.text: Describe the volume regulation of ADH secretion.
questions.explanation: Volume regulation overrides osmotic control during severe hypovolemia.
questions.keyConcept: Severe hypovolemia strongly stimulates ADH.
questions.modelAnswer: Hypovolemia (>15‑25% blood loss) reduces atrial stretch receptor activity → removes tonic inhibition → increases ADH release. Baroreceptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch also stimulate ADH. ADH then promotes water retention and vasoconstriction to restore volume.

questions.text: Compare between central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
questions.explanation: Differentiating test: desmopressin administration.
questions.keyConcept: Central DI responds to synthetic ADH; nephrogenic does not.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Central DI | Nephrogenic DI |
|---------|------------|----------------|
| Cause | ADH deficiency (hypothalamus/pituitary lesion) | Kidney unresponsive to ADH (V2 receptor or aquaporin defect) |
| Plasma ADH | Low | Normal/high |
| Response to desmopressin | Corrects polyuria | No response |

questions.text: Discuss the regulation of prolactin secretion.
questions.explanation: Dopamine is the primary regulator.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine inhibits prolactin; suckling overrides it.
questions.modelAnswer: Under tonic inhibition by dopamine (prolactin‑inhibiting factor, PIF) from hypothalamus. Prolactin‑releasing factors include TRH, VIP, and suckling-induced reflex. Estrogen increases prolactin secretion. Negative feedback: prolactin stimulates hypothalamic dopamine release.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a function of the endocrine system?
questions.explanation: Transmission of external stimuli is a function of the nervous system, not the endocrine system.
options: Regulation of metabolic activity, water and electrolyte balance.
Helping the body cope with stressful situations.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones is largely unbound to plasma proteins?
questions.explanation: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) circulates freely, not bound to carrier proteins, unlike steroid and thyroid hormones.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus directly controls the posterior pituitary via axonal projections (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei).
options: Secrets only releasing factors from its median eminence.
Has no control on the suprarenal medulla.
Releases the trophic hormones that control the gonadal functions.
Controls the neurohypophysis through a direct nervous connection.

questions.text: The neurohypophysis releases:
questions.explanation: The posterior pituitary releases vasopressin (ADH) and oxytocin.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding growth hormone?
questions.explanation: GH binds to its receptor, which activates JAK-STAT pathway (tyrosine kinase-associated).
options: Its secretion is inhibited by glucagon.
It acts by activating tyrosine kinase receptors.

questions.text: Which of the following conditions or hormones would most likely increase growth hormone (GH) secretion?
questions.explanation: Exercise, stress, hypoglycemia, and sleep increase GH secretion.

questions.text: Acromegaly is:
questions.explanation: GH excess causes insulin resistance, leading to hyperglycemia, and increased lipolysis (FFA).
options: Accompanied by increased blood glucose and free fatty acids.
Due to basophil adenoma in the pituitary during the adult life.
Due to ability of the liver to produce somatomedin.
Due to excess growth hormone (GH) secretion during infancy.
Accompanied by overgrowth of long bones.

questions.text: A Pituitary Dwarf is characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Pituitary dwarfism results in proportionate short stature with normal intelligence and sexual development (if gonadotropins intact).
options: Disproportionate retardation of bone and soft tissue growth.
Symmetrical retardation of bone and soft tissue growth.

questions.text: Which of the following represents the function of Prolactin hormone?
questions.explanation: Hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH, leading to amenorrhea and infertility.
options: Inhibits the growth of breast tissue.
In excess can produce amenorrhea in females.

questions.text: Which of the following inhibits prolactin secretion?
questions.explanation: Dopamine is the primary inhibitor of prolactin; dopamine agonists (bromocriptine) suppress prolactin.

questions.text: Effects of Vasopressin include which of the following?
questions.explanation: ADH increases water permeability by inserting aquaporin-2 channels in collecting ducts.

Decreasing the number of aquaporin in tubular cells.
Decreasing the flow of urea into medullary interstitium.
Strong vasoconstriction through binding V2 receptors.
Decreasing ACTH release from the anterior pituitary.

questions.text: Which of the following will stimulate the release of Antidiuretic (ADH) hormone?
questions.explanation: Hypovolemia (hemorrhage) is a potent stimulus for ADH release via baroreceptors.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about the releasing hormones produced in the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: Releasing hormones are secreted by neurosecretory cells in the median eminence into the portal circulation.
options: Are secreted by cells in the median eminence.
Pass down nerve axons to reach the pituitary gland.
Control the output of only one pituitary hormone.
Regulate the release of thyroxine from the thyroid gland.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin)?
questions.explanation: ADH secretion is primarily regulated by osmolality, but severe hypovolemia overrides osmolality to maintain volume.
options: Is formed and released from nerve endings in the posterior pituitary gland.
Tends to raise the osmolality of plasma.
Increases the permeability of the cells in the loop of Henle to water.
Secretion is little affected by changes in plasma osmolality of less than 10 per cent.
Secretion increases when plasma volume falls but osmolality is unchanged.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about prolactin?
questions.explanation: Suckling stimulates prolactin release via inhibition of dopamine.
options: Has a similar chemical structure and physiological action to luteinizing hormone.
Is responsible for breast growth in puberty.
Secretion is stimulated by suckling of the breast.
Causes pre-formed milk to be ejected by the breast during suckling.

questions.text: Excessive secretion of growth hormone (GH) before the fusion of the epiphyseal plates during puberty leads to which clinical condition?
questions.explanation: Prepubertal GH excess causes gigantism (excessive linear growth).

questions.text: Increased secretion of growth hormone before puberty leads to:
questions.explanation: Same as above: gigantism.

questions.text: Excess growth hormone secretion in adults may cause:
questions.explanation: Adult GH excess causes acromegaly with disproportionate growth of hands, feet, and face.

questions.text: Increased secretion of growth hormone after puberty may lead to:
questions.explanation: Postpubertal GH excess causes acromegaly.

questions.text: A 7-year-old boy has increased secretion of growth hormone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prepubertal GH excess → gigantism.

questions.text: An adult male suffered from increase in bone size which is limited to the bones of his hands, feet and face. Growth hormone level was increased. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acromegaly is characterized by enlargement of acral parts (hands, feet, face).

questions.text: In the previous case, which of the following cells are responsible for this clinical condition?
questions.explanation: Acromegaly results from somatotroph adenoma after epiphyseal closure.

questions.text: A young child suffered from abnormally tall stature, abnormal growth of the face, hands and feet and thickened facial features. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prepubertal GH excess causes gigantism; acromegalic features may also appear if excess continues after puberty.

questions.text: In the previous case, which of the following cells are responsible for this clinical condition?
questions.explanation: Gigantism is caused by somatotroph overactivity before epiphyseal closure.

questions.text: A patient presents with enlarged hands, feet, and coarse facial features. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Enlargement of acral parts is classic for acromegaly.

questions.text: What is the result of increased growth hormone secretion after puberty?
questions.explanation: Postpubertal GH excess → acromegaly.
options: Dwarfism due to premature epiphyseal closure
Gigantism from continued longitudinal bone growth

questions.text: Growth hormone (GH) is best described as:

questions.text: The secretion of which anterior pituitary hormone is tonically inhibited by dopamine from the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: Dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits prolactin secretion.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Prolactin is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Prolactin is tonically inhibited by dopamine, not stimulated by a PRH under normal conditions.
options: Its secretion is primarily inhibited by dopamine.
It is essential for milk production.
Tonically, its secretion is under the effect of Prolactin-releasing hormone.
High levels can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes prolactin?
questions.explanation: Prolactin acts directly on breast tissue, not on another endocrine gland, so it is not a tropic hormone.

It is a tropic hormone that regulates adrenal cortex function
It is a regulatory hormone released from the anterior pituitary that does not control an endocrine gland
It inhibits FSH and LH release through negative feedback on the hypothalamus
It is synthesized in the hypothalamus and transported to the anterior pituitary

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding the functions of the posterior pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, which causes milk ejection.
options: It synthesizes releasing hormones that control the anterior pituitary.
It secretes a hormone responsible for stimulating milk ejection.
It acts as the primary site of synthesis for antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
It produces prolactin to stimulate milk production in the mammary glands.
It releases hormones that directly regulate blood calcium levels.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones is classified as a neurohormone released directly from the posterior pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin (ADH) is a neurohormone synthesized in hypothalamus and released from posterior pituitary.

questions.text: Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) primarily acts on which specific segment of the nephron to facilitate the reabsorption of water and increase urine concentration?
questions.explanation: ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting ducts, especially the inner medullary portion, to insert aquaporin-2 channels.
options: Ascending limb of the Loop of Henle

questions.text: ADH increases water reabsorption mainly by acting on:
questions.explanation: The inner medullary collecting duct is the primary site for ADH-mediated water reabsorption.

questions.text: A decrease in pressure within the right atrium leads to an increased secretion of which hormone?
questions.explanation: Decreased atrial pressure (low blood volume) stimulates ADH release via baroreceptors.

questions.text: What physiological response occurs when right atrial pressure decreases?
questions.explanation: Low atrial pressure (hypovolemia) increases ADH to conserve water.
options: Decreased renin release from juxtaglomerular cells
Suppressed thirst center activity in the hypothalamus

questions.text: A young man suffers from polyuria (increased micturition), polydipsia (feels thirsty) and wakes often at night. Investigation reveals deficiency in ADH. Which of the following diseases best describes this case?
questions.explanation: Central diabetes insipidus results from ADH deficiency, causing polyuria and polydipsia.

questions.text: Diabetes insipidus is NOT:
questions.explanation: Diabetes insipidus is due to posterior pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction, not anterior lobe destruction.
options: Due to destruction of the anterior lobe of pituitary gland
Due to decreased secretion of ADH
Characterised by low specific gravity of urine

questions.text: What is the primary physiological stimulus for the release of adrenal androgens, such as DHEA?
questions.explanation: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce androgens as well as cortisol.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of positive feedback control?
questions.explanation: Estrogen stimulates the LH surge (positive feedback) leading to ovulation.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes a mechanism in which a hormone stimulates further release of the same or another hormone?
questions.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies the release of a hormone, e.g., oxytocin during labor, LH surge.

questions.text: When a target endocrine gland hormone inhibits the release of its corresponding tropic hormone from the pituitary, this is called:
questions.explanation: Long-loop feedback: peripheral hormone inhibits pituitary tropic hormone release.

questions.text: When a hormone secreted by a peripheral target organ inhibits the release of its corresponding tropic hormone from the anterior pituitary, this is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Long-loop feedback involves target gland hormone feedback to pituitary/hypothalamus.

questions.text: Which of the following terms describes the feedback mechanism where a hormone from a peripheral target organ inhibits the release of its tropic hormone from the anterior pituitary?
questions.explanation: Long-loop feedback: e.g., cortisol inhibits ACTH.

questions.text: A process in which a secreted hormone acts upon the exact same cell that produced it is termed:
questions.explanation: Autocrine signaling: cell responds to its own secreted molecule.

questions.text: The phenomenon whereby one hormone must be present in adequate amounts to allow a second hormone to exert its full effect is known as:
questions.explanation: Permissiveness: e.g., thyroid hormone permits catecholamine action.

questions.text: Which best defines the permissive action of a hormone?
questions.explanation: Permissiveness: one hormone enhances the responsiveness of a target to another hormone.
options: Two hormones act synergistically to produce an exaggerated response
A hormone binds to receptors and triggers a second messenger cascade
One hormone makes target cells more responsive to a second hormone
A hormone blocks the receptor site for another hormone
A hormone is secreted only when another hormone is present

questions.text: The main stimulus for oxytocin secretion is:
questions.explanation: Cervical dilation during labor triggers the Ferguson reflex, releasing oxytocin.

questions.text: Which of the following serves as a primary physiological stimulus for the secretion of oxytocin?
questions.explanation: Cervical stretch stimulates oxytocin release.

questions.text: What is the primary action of oxytocin?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin causes uterine contractions during labor and milk ejection, but its primary obstetric action is uterine contraction.

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary physiological function of oxytocin?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin causes myoepithelial cell contraction, ejecting milk.
options: Reabsorption of water in the renal collecting ducts
Stimulation of milk synthesis in the alveolar cells
Contraction of the myoepithelial cells for milk ejection

questions.text: What is the function of oxytocin?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is responsible for milk ejection, not milk production (prolactin does that).
options: Stimulates milk production in the mammary glands
Promotes water reabsorption in the collecting ducts
Stimulates thyroid hormone release from the thyroid gland
Milk ejection (let-down reflex) from the mammary glands
Increases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle

questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Laboratory tests show elevated serum prolactin levels. Which of the following is the most likely associated finding?
questions.explanation: Hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH, leading to infertility and amenorrhea.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones are inhibited by the action of Melatonin?
questions.explanation: Melatonin inhibits GnRH secretion, thus delaying puberty.

questions.text: Which of the following is a stimulus for increasing oxytocin secretion?
questions.explanation: Cervical dilatation triggers oxytocin release.

questions.text: A patient with a pituitary adenoma subsequently suffers an acute adrenal crisis (Addisonian crisis). Biopsy of the adrenal glands reveals an atrophied cortex but a preserved zona glomerulosa. What is the primary cause of this adrenal atrophy?
questions.explanation: Pituitary tumor compresses normal corticotrophs, reducing ACTH and causing secondary adrenal atrophy. Zona glomerulosa is preserved because it is mainly regulated by renin-angiotensin.

questions.text: A patient presents with neurological symptoms. Imaging reveals a pituitary adenoma. Further examination and blood work show a decrease in the size of the adrenal glands. This adrenal atrophy is likely due to:
questions.explanation: Decreased ACTH due to pituitary tumor mass effect leads to adrenal atrophy.

questions.text: Which of the following changes would most likely occur following administration of a high dose of glucocorticoids?
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on the pituitary and hypothalamus, decreasing ACTH.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones primarily stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoids?
questions.explanation: ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion from the zona fasciculata.

questions.text: Which organ is primarily responsible for producing somatomedins in response to growth hormone stimulation?
questions.explanation: The liver produces IGF-1 (somatomedin) in response to GH.

questions.text: Which of the following is the main action of IGF-1?
questions.explanation: IGF-1 mediates the effects of GH on cartilage growth (maturation and proliferation).
options: Increases cortisol secretion from adrenal cortex

questions.text: Which of the following statements accurately characterises the primary mechanism of action for lipophilic hormones, such as steroid and thyroid hormones?
questions.explanation: Lipophilic hormones diffuse into cells, bind intracellular/nuclear receptors, and modulate gene transcription.
options: They activate adenylyl cyclase to increase intracellular cAMP.
They bind exclusively to cell surface G-protein coupled receptors.
They alter gene transcription after binding to their specific receptor.
They require extensive second messenger cascades to function.
They are stored in large secretory vesicles prior to release.

questions.text: What is true about lipophilic hormones?
questions.explanation: Lipophilic hormones act via nuclear receptors to affect transcription.
options: Affecting gene transcription after receptor binding

questions.text: Through which intracellular mechanism do cholera and pertussis toxins primarily exert their pathological effects?
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs, constitutively activating adenylyl cyclase; pertussis toxin inactivates Gi, also leading to increased cAMP.
options: Cleavage of the phospholipase C enzyme.
Direct phosphorylation of protein kinase A.

questions.text: How do Cholera and pertussis toxins exert their effect?
questions.explanation: Both toxins ultimately cause persistent activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased cAMP.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones initiates its intracellular signalling cascade via the Janus kinase/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway?
questions.explanation: GH receptor is a cytokine receptor that activates JAK2, leading to STAT phosphorylation.

questions.text: Which hormone acts through the JAK-STAT signaling pathway?
questions.explanation: GH uses JAK-STAT; insulin uses receptor tyrosine kinase.

questions.text: Which signaling mechanism is primarily utilized by the Growth Hormone receptor?
questions.explanation: GHR is a JAK-STAT coupled receptor.

questions.text: Growth Hormone (GH) exerts its effects primarily through which signaling pathway/second messenger system?
questions.explanation: JAK-STAT is the primary pathway for GH.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding the insulin receptor?
questions.explanation: The insulin receptor β-subunit has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity.

The receptor utilizes a G-protein coupled mechanism to activate adenylyl cyclase.
The α-subunit directly phosphorylates intracellular target proteins.
The β-subunit possesses intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity.
The receptor relies on recruiting cytosolic Janus kinases (JAKs) upon activation.

questions.explanation: Insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase.

The alpha subunit acts directly as an intracellular ion channel.

The beta subunit possesses intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity.
It directly interacts with adenylate cyclase upon ligand binding.

questions.explanation: Insulin and IGF-1 receptors are tyrosine kinases.

questions.explanation: Correct order: G protein → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA.

questions.text: Glucagon exerts its primary metabolic effects by utilizing which of the following second messengers?
questions.explanation: Glucagon increases cAMP.

questions.text: What serves as the primary cellular receptor for nitric oxide (NO) within smooth muscle cells?
questions.explanation: NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase in the cytoplasm, increasing cGMP.

questions.text: What is the receptor for nitric oxide (NO)?
questions.explanation: NO receptor is soluble guanylyl cyclase.

questions.text: Nitric oxide (NO) exerts its effect via which receptor mechanism?
questions.explanation: NO activates cytoplasmic guanylate cyclase.

questions.text: Which enzyme is responsible for the specific cleavage of membrane phospholipids to form diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol triphosphate (IP3)?
questions.explanation: Phospholipase C (PLC) cleaves PIP2 into DAG and IP3.

questions.text: In cell signaling, which enzyme is responsible for the cleavage of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into the second messengers diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3)?
questions.explanation: PLC hydrolyzes PIP2.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones utilises cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as its primary second messenger for physiological action?
questions.explanation: ANP binds to guanylyl cyclase receptors, increasing cGMP.

questions.text: Which of the following signaling molecules exerts its physiological effects by increasing the intracellular levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)?
questions.explanation: ANF increases cGMP.

questions.text: Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) exerts its effects primarily by activating which second messenger system?
questions.explanation: ANF activates membrane-bound guanylyl cyclase (NPR-A).

questions.text: What is the primary membrane-bound enzyme activated by Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF) upon binding to its receptor?
questions.explanation: ANF receptor has intrinsic guanylyl cyclase activity.

questions.text: Which enzyme is responsible for the inhibition of the hormonal effect of cGMP by catalyzing its breakdown?
questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cGMP to GMP, terminating the signal.

questions.text: Which of the following features is a characteristic functional property of heterotrimeric G-proteins?
questions.explanation: G proteins hydrolyze GTP to GDP, acting as molecular switches.

They directly phosphorylate intracellular target proteins.
They are exclusively located within the cell nucleus.

questions.explanation: Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP.

questions.text: What is the primary downstream target activated directly by diacylglycerol (DAG) in the phosphoinositide signalling cascade?
questions.explanation: DAG activates protein kinase C (PKC).

questions.text: Which second messenger is directly activated by Diacylglycerol (DAG)?
questions.explanation: DAG activates PKC.

questions.text: Diacylglycerol's main action in second messenger systems:
questions.explanation: DAG activates PKC.

questions.text: Inositol triphosphate acts as a second messenger, as it can?
questions.explanation: IP3 binds to IP3 receptors on ER, causing Ca2+ release.

questions.text: Protein kinase A enzyme is activated by how many molecules of cAMP?
questions.explanation: Four cAMP molecules bind to two regulatory subunits, causing dissociation and activation of catalytic subunits.

questions.text: The volatile hormone NO is derived from which amino acid?
questions.explanation: NO is synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS).

questions.text: Describe clinical features of acromegaly.
questions.explanation: Excess GH after epiphyseal closure causes bony overgrowth and soft tissue enlargement.
questions.keyConcept: Acromegaly results from post-pubertal GH excess.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Enlarged hands and feet
- Protruding jaw (prognathism)
- Coarse facial features
- Organomegaly (heart, liver, kidneys)
- Kyphosis
- Hyperglycemia
- Possible visual defects from pituitary tumor compressing optic chiasma

questions.text: Compare between gigantism and acromegaly.
questions.explanation: Both caused by excess GH; timing determines whether linear growth or acral enlargement occurs.
questions.keyConcept: Open vs closed epiphyseal plates determine phenotype.
questions.modelAnswer:
Feature          | Gigantism                          | Acromegaly
Time of onset    | Before epiphyseal closure (childhood) | After epiphyseal closure (adulthood)
Primary effect   | Increased linear height            | Increased thickness of bones (hands, face, jaw)
Other features   | Proportionate enlargement          | Coarse features, organomegaly

questions.text: A 29-year-old primigravida has marked vaginal bleeding after the onset of labor. She remains hypotensive for 6 hours and requires transfusion of 12 packed RBC units. Postpartum, she becomes unable to breast-feed the infant. She does not have a resumption of normal menstrual cycles.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.

subQuestions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Pituitary necrosis (Sheehan's syndrome).
subQuestions.explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage leading to hypotension can cause ischemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary gland.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Sheehan's syndrome: pituitary infarction after massive postpartum hemorrhage.

subQuestions.text: What is the name of this syndrome?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Sheehan's syndrome.
subQuestions.explanation: Named after Harold Sheehan who described postpartum pituitary necrosis.

subQuestions.text: What are the other possible complications which may occur?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Pituitary myxedema (hypothyroidism due to lack of TSH) and atrophy of the sexual organs (due to lack of FSH and LH). Adrenal insufficiency may also occur.
subQuestions.explanation: Loss of anterior pituitary hormones leads to secondary hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, and adrenal insufficiency.

questions.text: What are the types of pituitary adenomas?
questions.explanation: Prolactinoma is the most frequent functioning type.
questions.keyConcept: Adenomas are benign but can cause mass effect or hormone excess.
questions.modelAnswer:
Functioning (hormone‑secreting):
- Prolactinoma (most common)
- GH‑secreting (gigantism/acromegaly)
- ACTH‑secreting (Cushing disease)
- TSH‑secreting (rare)
- Gonadotroph adenomas (FSH/LH, often nonfunctioning)
Nonfunctioning (null cell) adenomas – present with mass effect.

questions.text: Describe Sheehan's syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis).
questions.explanation: First sign is often inability to breastfeed.
questions.keyConcept: Sheehan's = pituitary infarction after obstetric hemorrhage.
questions.modelAnswer: Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum hemorrhage. Enlarged pituitary (from pregnancy) is vulnerable to hypotension. Results in panhypopituitarism: failure of lactation (prolactin), amenorrhea (FSH/LH), hypothyroidism (TSH), adrenal insufficiency (ACTH).

questions.text: List the causes of anterior pituitary hypofunction.
questions.explanation: Hypopituitarism may be gradual or acute.
questions.keyConcept: Mass, ischemia, infiltration, or autoimmunity.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas (compression)
- Sheehan syndrome
- Surgical or radiation ablation
- Infiltrative diseases (sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis)
- Pituitary apoplexy (hemorrhage into adenoma)
- Autoimmune hypophysitis
- Empty sella syndrome

questions.text: Compare between gigantism and acromegaly.
questions.explanation: Same hormone (GH) but different effects due to growth plate status.
questions.keyConcept: Open plates → gigantism; closed plates → acromegaly.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Gigantism | Acromegaly |
|---------|-----------|------------|
| Age of onset | Before epiphyseal closure (childhood) | After epiphyseal closure (adulthood) |
| Effect | Linear growth (tall stature) | Acral enlargement (hands, feet, jaw) |
| Facial features | Normal proportions | Coarse, prognathism |
| Organomegaly | Less prominent | Present |

questions.text: What is the clinical importance of posterior pituitary syndromes?
questions.explanation: Posterior pituitary disorders involve water balance.
questions.keyConcept: DI = ADH deficiency; SIADH = ADH excess.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency): polyuria, polydipsia, dilute urine.
- SIADH (inappropriate ADH secretion): hyponatremia, concentrated urine, fluid retention (due to tumors, CNS disorders, drugs).
Ectopic ADH production (e.g., small cell lung cancer) also causes SIADH.

questions.text: A 29‑year‑old primigravida has marked vaginal bleeding after the onset of labor. She remains hypotensive for 6 hours and requires transfusion of 12 packed RBC units. Postpartum, she becomes unable to breast‑feed the infant and does not resume normal menstrual cycles.
questions.explanation: Classic presentation of Sheehan syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Postpartum hemorrhage → pituitary infarction.

subQuestions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis).
subQuestions.explanation: Massive postpartum hemorrhage leads to ischemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary.

subQuestions.text: What are the expected hormonal deficiencies?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Deficiencies of GH, prolactin (→ failure to lactate), TSH (→ central hypothyroidism), ACTH (→ adrenal insufficiency), and FSH/LH (→ amenorrhea).
subQuestions.explanation: Destruction of anterior pituitary causes panhypopituitarism.

questions.text: Sheehan's syndrome is characterised by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome occurs in adults; growth and mental retardation are not features (those are from childhood hypopituitarism).
options: It is due to post-partum haemorrhage
Necrosis of the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland

questions.text: Post partum hemorrhagic necrosis of pituitary gland is called:
questions.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome is pituitary infarction after severe postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.text: A 22 year old female suffers from post partum haemorrhage following delivery of her second child. She delivers a normal term male infant. She overcomes this serious complication by strict medical care and blood transfusion. She was unlucky to discover her failure to lactate her baby. This is probably the result of:
questions.explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage can cause pituitary necrosis (Sheehan's), leading to prolactin deficiency and failure of lactation.

questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with acute onset of cessation of lactation. She delivered her first child a few months ago, and has been breast feeding since then. She also says that she has not menstruated since the delivery and lately she has been tired and always feeling cold. Laboratory workup reveals deficiency of ACTH and other anterior pituitary hormones. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's signs & symptoms?
questions.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome presents with postpartum panhypopituitarism, including ACTH deficiency and hypothyroidism.

questions.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia is:
questions.explanation: MEN syndromes are autosomal dominant.

questions.text: Pituitary adenomas may have no hormonal effects. (True/False)
questions.explanation: Non-functioning pituitary adenomas do not secrete hormones.

questions.text: Hyperpituitarism may lead to gigantism or acromegaly depending on the level of growth hormone. (True/False)
questions.explanation: It depends on the age of onset (prepubertal vs postpubertal), not the level of GH per se.

questions.text: A 49-year-old man who smokes two packs of cigarettes a day presents with a lung mass on x-ray and recent weight gain. Laboratory examination reveals hyponatremia with hyperosmolar urine. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these clinical findings?
questions.explanation: Small cell lung cancer can cause SIADH, leading to hyponatremia and concentrated urine.

questions.text: A female patient presents with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. What is the most likely underlying pathological cause?
questions.explanation: Prolactinoma causes galactorrhea and amenorrhea.

questions.text: What is the classic aetiology of Sheehan's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Sheehan's = postpartum pituitary infarction.
options: Autoimmune destruction of the posterior pituitary
Ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary gland following severe postpartum haemorrhage
Haemorrhage into a pre-existing pituitary macroadenoma
Congenital hypoplasia of the Rathke's pouch

questions.text: List adverse effects of octreotide.

questions.keyConcept: Somatostatin analogs cause biliary and GI side effects.
